items.title: 27.5.3 The Genetic Code and Protein Synthesis

source_refs.note: Topic 27.5.3 with Quick Check 27.4, answered (PDF 174); Figures 27.14 and 27.17 are redrawn. The book's comparison box asks the questions only; answers were derived and need review.

blocks.text: Protein synthesis transfers the genetic information encoded in DNA into proteins. It starts with replication, making copies of DNA. In the nucleus the genetic instructions for making a protein are copied from a DNA gene into mRNA: this is transcription. The completed mRNA strand leaves the DNA and enters the cytoplasm, where it attaches to ribosomes. At the ribosomes the code carried by mRNA is read and converted into a specific sequence of amino acids: this is translation. tRNA molecules bring the amino acids in the order of the bases (codons, groups of three bases) in the mRNA, the amino acids join in a chain, and the growing polypeptide becomes the complete protein.

blocks.alt: Top: five boxes, genome (all the DNA, in the nucleus), chromosome (23 pairs in a human cell), gene (a section of DNA for one protein), DNA (bases on a sugar-phosphate chain) and codon (three bases code for one amino acid). Bottom: DNA -> DNA by replication (DNA polymerase), DNA -> mRNA by transcription (RNA polymerase) in the nucleus, and mRNA -> protein by translation (ribosome and tRNA) in the cytoplasm.
blocks.caption: From the genome to the codon, and the flow of genetic information (original diagram after Figures 27.14 and 27.17).
blocks.long_description: Information is stored in the order of bases in DNA, organised as genes on chromosomes. To make a protein, a gene is transcribed into mRNA, which leaves the nucleus; at the ribosome each codon of three bases is matched by a tRNA carrying one particular amino acid, so the base sequence becomes an amino acid sequence.
